item.title: Stocks and Bonds Steady at the End of a Tumultuous Week
item.description:
Markets regained a measure of calm in early trading on Friday, with stocks rising slightly and bonds trading flat.

It has been a bruising week, with investors’ fears about the war in Iran, government deficits, the state of the economy and a deluge of A.I. debt coming to a head. This confluence hit the bond market particularly hard, although signs of stress could also be seen in stocks, currencies and commodities.

A surprising midweek move by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to ease stress in the bond market has already mostly faded, with yields springing back to where they were before the intervention, near multi-decade highs. Stocks remain on track for a weekly decline. The combination of a fall in the value of the dollar and a jump in the price of gold suggests that investors are anxious about the path of U.S. fiscal policy.

Government bond yields were little changed in early trading on Friday. The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury, which has been the focus of investor angst about inflation, deficits and A.I.-related borrowing, was flat at 5.24 percent.

The 10-year Treasury yield, a vital benchmark for mortgages, business loans and other types of debt, traded at just under 4.7 percent.

After U.S. government bond yields hit multi-decade highs earlier this week, Mr. Bessent calmed the market by doubling the amount of debt the Treasury Department is permitted to buy back from investors. The effect of the move didn’t last long: Yields are now largely back to where they were before the intervention.

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

Futures on the S&P 500 pointed to a rise when stocks resume trading in the United States on Friday. But after several choppy trading sessions the benchmark index is on track for a weekly decline, after posting increases in the previous three weeks.

In Europe, the Stoxx 600, a broad-index that tracks the region’s largest companies, was flat.

Stocks in Asia mostly rose. The Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong rose 1.2 percent. The Nikkei 225 in Japan dipped 0.3 percent.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, fluctuated between small gains and losses, hovering around $94 a barrel. The cost of crude has risen nearly 30 percent since the start of the war. This week, President Trump promised an “economic D-Day” against Iran, suggesting dim prospects for an end to the conflict.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, traded at about $87 a barrel.

Investors and analysts are focused on the continued disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that is a vital trading route for oil and natural gas. Over the last month, the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen have restricted traffic in the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, which Saudi Arabia has used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

On Thursday, 10 ships navigated the Strait of Hormuz and 32 vessels moved through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to Kpler, a maritime data firm. Traffic through both waterways was slightly lower than the most recent five-day average. Passages through the Strait of Hormuz continue to run at a small fraction of prewar levels.

The New York Times

Gas prices rose again on Friday, up slightly to a national average of $4.11 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club. The price at the pump has risen by 38 percent since the war began.

Gas prices don’t move in lock step with crude, usually trailing increases or drops by a few days.

The average price of diesel increased to $5.58 per gallon on Friday, up 48 percent since the start of the war.

Here is a county-level look at where drivers are facing the highest costs.

“The debasement trade is powered by the fear that fiscal policy across many advanced economies is out of control,” Robin J. Brooks wrote on Substack on Friday. “Markets fear that governments will be tempted to inflate away unsustainable debt burdens.” He is a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

The so-called debasement trade describes a rush to safe assets by investors who are concerned, in part, about the prospect of higher inflation. Gold, a haven during times of turmoil, is on track for a weekly gain of about 5 percent. Silver is set for an even bigger weekly gain of more than 7 percent.

item.title: Trump Widens Beef Imports in Bid to Lower Prices
item.description:
President Trump will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to be imported into the United States with lower tariffs over the next 90 days, he said in a social media post on Friday morning, a bid to lower the cost of a staple food for Americans pinched by higher prices.

The beef will be imported with “no out of quota tariff” and sold 25 percent below the current market price, which is $6.89 per pound, he said.

The president provided almost no details about how his plan would work. It seemed to surprise and anger ranchers. He did not say what countries this beef would come from, where it would be sold or how it would be sold for 25 percent off.

A White House official said the president would sign an executive order to remove the tariffs within the next two weeks. In exchange for the tariff relief, the president had secured a deal with foreign beef exporters to provide a 25 percent discount, he said.

The official did not specify which foreign exporters he was referring to, or which country the beef was from.

“This action, during a time of record high demand for beef, will help address the affordability of beef, after our nation’s cattle supply fell to its lowest level in 75 years under the Biden administration,” the Agriculture Department said.

Groups representing ranchers said the plan was only a short-term fix for consumers, and would hurt ranchers and discourage them from increasing the supply of American cattle and reducing prices over the longer term.

“While America’s cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd,” said Colin Woodall, the chief executive of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association.

He pointed out that the market price for live cattle fell after the president’s announcement, already costing ranchers money.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly implemented tariffs in an effort to protect U.S. markets, raise revenue for the U.S. government and goad foreign countries into making concessions. But the levies have also pushed up U.S. consumer prices, according to economists, crashing headlong into Mr. Trump’s promises to help alleviate the cost of living for Americans.

The White House has struggled to address persistently high grocery prices, especially high beef prices. Since Mr. Trump returned to office in January 2025, the price of ground beef has risen 24 percent, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The only durable way to lower beef prices, ranchers and economists said, is to increase the size of the American cattle herd. U.S. cattle numbers are the smallest since the 1950s, after years of drought and low margins caused cattle producers to reduce the size of their herds or leave the business. It takes years for ranchers to increase the size of the country’s herd, and there is little evidence they have taken steps to do so over the past 18 months.

“Today’s announcement and other market interventions throw cold water on the prospect of herd expansion and sacrifices long-term stability for short-term messaging,” Mr. Woodall said.

Earlier this year, the president signed an executive order to allow imports of an additional 80,000 metric tons of ground beef from Argentina without tariffs.

Last year, the United States imported almost 1.9 million metric tons of beef and beef products, according to Census Bureau trade data. More than 80 percent of the beef Americans consume is produced in the United States, meaning that even an increase in beef imports is unlikely to radically increase the supply of beef and lower prices.

Another small increase in the beef supply could be on the horizon. Live cattle imports from Mexico were halted in May 2025 over fears of the spread of the flesh-eating screwworm fly. But with the fly having reached the United States this summer, the Agriculture Department plans to slowly reopen the southern border to Mexican cattle starting on Monday.

item.title: Meghan of Sussex Eyes a Role in a Netflix Show
item.description:
In Hollywood, it qualifies as a “possible maybe” with an asterisk — perhaps two.

Representatives for Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in the show business capital have had exploratory talks about her joining a third season of “The Gentlemen,” Guy Ritchie’s Netflix crime series, according to two people briefed on the discussions, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because no deal had been consummated.

One important caveat: Netflix has not yet ordered a third season of “The Gentlemen.”

Netflix declined to comment, as did Toff Guy Films, one of the production companies behind the series. The publicity firm Sunshine Sachs, which represents Meghan, declined to comment.

The discussions, however preliminary, represent another step toward an acting comeback for Meghan, 45, who left the drama “Suits” in 2017 as her relationship with Prince Harry became increasingly serious. She recently returned to acting with a cameo in the forthcoming Amazon MGM movie “Close Personal Friends.”

It was her first role in more than seven years and will debut on their service next year. Meghan’s enormous celebrity greatly complicates her casting, production executives have said: It’s difficult for audiences to see a character rather than the Duchess of Sussex.

“The Gentlemen” could offer a considerably splashier return, depending on the size of the role. The series, created by Ritchie and based on his 2019 movie of the same name, follows an English aristocrat who discovers that his family estate houses a sprawling marijuana operation.

The first season was a breakout hit for Netflix, spending three weeks as the streaming service’s most-watched English-language television series worldwide. The second season, starring Theo James, debuts on Sept. 3.

The series films in Britain. The potential job may offer a clue behind the abrupt decision revealed this week by Harry and Meghan to move their family back to the country after six years in self-exile in the United States during a royal rift with Harry’s family.

The news of Harry and Meghan’s return set off a media feeding frenzy. They couple and their many dramas have polarized the public but still command intense interest. The possibility of Meghan having an acting job was earlier reported by News.com.au, an Australian news organization, and separately in a Substack post by Tina Brown, the former editor in chief of Tatler, Vanity Fair and The New Yorker.

So, to recap: Meghan is in early talks for an unidentified role in a season of television that does not yet exist.

Hollywood has greenlit projects on less.

Michael D. Shear contributed reporting.

item.title: Overlooked No More: Patricia Douglas, Who Challenged Hollywood’s Culture of Abuse
item.description:
This article is part of Overlooked, a series of obituaries about remarkable people whose deaths, beginning in 1851, went unreported in The Times.

In May 1937, a 20-year-old extra and dancer named Patricia Douglas was invited to appear in a movie produced by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, the biggest movie studio in Hollywood.

When she showed up on location at the ranch of the producer Hal Roach in Culver City, Calif., she discovered that there was no film shoot. Instead, she later said, she and more than 100 other young women — many of whom were minors — had been summoned to entertain men attending MGM’s annual sales convention.

Douglas later testified in court that during the event, one MGM salesman harassed her, then two men held her down and forced her to drink liquor. Later, she said, the salesman assaulted and raped her in the parking lot.

She reported the attack to prosecutors, pursued a criminal case and sued the studio executives she believed were responsible. She later said MGM mounted a campaign to discredit her, and witnesses mysteriously recanted their earlier statements. A grand jury declined to indict the salesman, her civil suit was dismissed and her story fell out of public memory.

Douglas later said MGM had mounted a campaign to discredit her and had succeeded, and she was blackballed by Hollywood. Years before the #MeToo movement of the late 2010s transformed the way sexual abuse in Hollywood was discussed, Douglas’s story re-emerged because of a curious reporter who had happened upon the case in the course of other research.

“I see her as the Rosa Parks of rape culture,” David Stenn, the reporter, said in an interview. “She stood up against the culture of silence when no one else did.”

Stenn unearthed Douglas’s story in 2003 for a Vanity Fair article, “It Happened One Night at MGM,” and a 2007 film documentary, “Girl 27,” a title taken from the number assigned to Douglas in MGM’s call sheet for the supposed movie shoot — a document he discovered in the Hal Roach archives at the University of Southern California.

Stenn researched the Douglas case for years, digging up grand jury affidavits with sworn testimonies, along with black-and-white film footage of the salesmen arriving at the ranch, where they were welcomed by MGM’s studio chief, Louis B. Mayer. The event was billed as a Wild West show, and the women were given cowgirl costumes to wear.

Karen McNally, the editor of the 2026 book “Women in Hollywood’s Dream Factory: Tales of Inequality, Abuse, and Resistance,” said in an interview that the circumstances surrounding Douglas’s assault were hardly unusual in the 1930s studio system. Young women were routinely brought in to entertain men at industry events, leaving them vulnerable to abuse, she said.

“If you’re repeating the behavior in this manner, which is quite blatant and intentional — that’s a system,” she said.

Patricia Douglas was born Dorothy Shellenberger on March 24, 1917, in Kansas City, Mo., to William Shellenberger, a chauffeur, and Mildred Kritser, who Douglas later estimated had been “married eight times.”

The family moved to Los Angeles in 1920; her parents divorced in 1928. Kritser was a gown designer who “kind of disappeared,” Douglas said, moving into an apartment in Beverly Hills while Dorothy went to live with her grandparents.

At the time, young women from across the country were flocking to Los Angeles, lured by the promise of Hollywood and the opportunities it seemed to offer, especially amid the Great Depression.

“It’s kind of like, ‘Go west, young woman!’ because women have opportunities in Hollywood that they don’t have in other places,” said McNally, who is a professor of American film, television and cultural history at London Metropolitan University. “It’s advertised as something new and wonderful. These young women would have been running around auditioning everywhere.”

At around 14, Dorothy dropped out of school to work as a dancer and changed her name to Patricia Douglas. At 16, she appeared, uncredited, in the 1933 Bert Wheeler-Robert Woolsey comedy “So This Is Africa” and the musical “Gold Diggers of 1933.”

Douglas was in her mid-80s when Stenn tracked her down in Las Vegas, where she was living at the time. With her permission, he recorded their phone conversations for months. He eventually persuaded her to sit for an on-camera interview in 2002.

She told Stenn that the party hosted by MGM was on May 5, 1937, the final night of a four-day convention. A Chicago-based salesman named David Ross approached Douglas on the dance floor. “He kept pestering me to teach him how to truck,” she said. “That was the dance at the time.” He tried every way he could “to get his hands around me,” and eventually she left the dance floor and returned to her table.

There were cases of scotch and champagne, but when Douglas said she didn’t drink alcohol, two salesmen forced her to, by holding her nose and pouring the liquor into her mouth.

She ran to the washroom to vomit, then went out to the parking lot for air. That was when Ross knocked her down, dragged her to his car and raped her, she said.

“The only thing I can remember is this David Ross’s face. It was in my nightmares for many years,” she said in the film documentary. “I could not get him off my mind and what he had done to me. He took my innocence. You can never get that back.”

Her account of the incident became headline news almost immediately after it happened. The Daily Times, a Chicago tabloid paper, ran a full-page headline, “Wild Film Party,” and a sub-headline, “Assault Told by Girl, 17,” for a story that included her name and photo, incorrectly reporting her age as three years younger than she was.

Subsequent news about developments in the case appeared in papers across the country, including The Los Angeles Times, with stories resorting to euphemisms like “ravished” or “outraged” instead of “rape.”

“Rape was literally a four-letter word in the 1930s,” Stenn said. “They wouldn’t print it in the newspapers."

Ross called Douglas’s claims “absurd, ridiculous” and Mayer’s personal attorney defended the salesman in the case, Stenn said.

When the grand jury declined to indict Ross, Douglas refused to let the matter end there. She sued Ross and other studio executives in Los Angeles Superior Court, accusing them of conspiring to “defile, debauch, and seduce” her for “the immoral and sensual gratification of male guests,” according to legal documents. She sought $500,000 in damages — more than $11 million in today’s dollars.

The suit was dismissed in February 1938. The next day, she filed an identical suit in federal court, arguing that the assault had violated her civil rights. It was, Stenn wrote in Vanity Fair, apparently the first time a woman had made rape the basis of a federal civil-rights case. That case, too, was ultimately dismissed because both lawyers failed to show up in court.

In “Girl 27,” Stenn described a cover-up campaign led by executives at MGM, which implicated the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s office and the doctor who had examined Douglas after the attack. Even an eyewitness who had helped her when she emerged from the bushes, crying and bleeding, later denied having seen anything.

“What she did had no real precedent, and she did it in a vacuum when there was no support on any level, no legal protections for women, and such a situation was considered unspeakable,” Stenn said in an interview.

A representative from Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns MGM’s film library from the 1930s, said the company did not have “anyone who can speak on the matter.” The Los Angeles County District Attorney’s office could not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Douglas married and divorced three times and had a daughter from her first marriage. Douglas died on Nov. 11, 2003, in Las Vegas. She was 86.

McNally said that very few cases of harassment and assault in the film industry came to light at the time, unless the woman involved was famous. Although there’s evidence that stars like Lana Turner, Judy Garland, and Shirley Temple faced sexual harassment or assault on the job, those stories often went public long after the incidents occurred.

The fact that Douglas’s case became so widely known was also unusual, McNally said. “Her case was in the press at the time,” she said. “It was headline news, and it was out there at the time, and then just forgotten.”

item.title: Boeing Engineers and Technicians Reject Contract Offer
item.description:
More than two-thirds of a union representing engineers and technicians at Boeing voted on Friday to reject the latest contract offer from the aircraft manufacturer, and signed off on a potential strike action if their current contract expires in October without a replacement.

Members of the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace rejected Boeing’s proposal of a nearly 30 percent rise in wages over four years, despite its unanimous endorsement by the union’s negotiating committee. The wage increase would have been the group’s largest since 1983, the union said.

In a statement, the union, which represents roughly 17,000 Boeing workers, said the vote underscored a deep distrust between its members and corporate management.

“It’s important to acknowledge how we got here; this mistrust was built brick by brick over the past several contracts,” the union negotiators said in a statement.

A Boeing vice president, Ben Nimmergut, said the company was disappointed with the vote.

“We gave a strong contract offer to position our employees among the market leaders in pay and benefits in the Pacific Northwest,” Mr. Nimmergut, the company’s functional chief engineer for production engineering, said in a statement. “We are now implementing our strike contingency plan,” he added.

Union negotiators will canvass members to better understand what is needed to get the contract passed, with the aim of securing a new deal before the current contract runs out on Oct. 6, the union’s statement said.

“However, we also are prepared to call for a labor stoppage, based on the overwhelming support of our members for the strike authorization vote,” the union said.

Boeing has dealt with other strikes in recent years. About 33,000 Boeing workers who mostly build commercial planes in the Seattle area went on strike for nearly two months in 2024 before reaching a deal and returning to work. The next year, about 3,200 Boeing workers who build fighter jets and weapons in the St. Louis area were on strike for more than three months before approving a new contract.
